title: Contingent valuation

definition.text: A survey-based technique for putting a money value on things that are not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution.

facts.text: The survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity, or how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss.
It is called a stated preference method, as opposed to revealed preference methods that rely on prices people actually pay.
Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed the idea in theory in 1947, and Robert K. Davis first applied it in 1963 to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists.
It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s, when governments gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values.
The Exxon Valdez oil spill was the first case where its surveys were used to put numbers on damages.
Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits, and many economists prefer evidence from real market purchases.
US government departments have used it widely in cost-benefit analyses of projects that affect the environment, such as valuing river recreation below Glen Canyon dam.
Clive Spash's research found that many willingness-to-pay answers behaved like charitable donations rather than the trade prices economists assumed.

contested_note: Many economists doubt that survey answers about willingness to pay reflect real values, while defenders say newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

definition.text: A panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, convened by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to judge whether contingent valuation surveys could be trusted.

facts.text: It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993.
It recommended personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum format on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats.
Preferring cautious estimates, it advised measuring willingness to pay to protect a good rather than willingness to accept its loss.
It judged that well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values.

title: Ecosystem valuation

definition.text: The process of assigning a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides.

facts.text: Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage is meant to help policy-makers compare policies through cost-benefit analysis.
In 1997 Robert Costanza and colleagues made the first estimate of the worldwide worth of ecosystem services: $33 trillion a year.
It draws on stated preference methods such as contingent valuation and revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost.
TEEB found ecosystem service values ranging from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded and may be non-rival and non-excludable.
Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and the money value society gives to services depends on how income is distributed.
Some programmes go on to pay landowners for services; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests.

related: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
contested_note: Sources describe ecosystem valuation as philosophically and ethically controversial, with debate over whether nature should be priced at all.

definition.text: A revealed preference method that values a place without a market price, such as a national park or beach, from what visitors spend in time and money to get there.

facts.text: Harold Hotelling suggested it in a 1947 letter to the US National Park Service; Trice and Wood (1958) and Clawson (1959) refined it.
People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often, while those nearby visit more and spend less.
Visitors are grouped into distance zones, each zone's visit rate is regressed on travel cost, and the result builds a demand curve for the site.
The area under that demand curve gives willingness to pay for the site, used as its value in cost-benefit analysis.

definition.text: The smallest amount of money a person would take to sell a good or service, or to put up with a harm such as pollution.

facts.text: It is the counterpart of willingness to pay, the most a buyer would give up to get something or avoid something unwanted; both are reservation prices.
A trade's price falls between the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's willingness to accept, and the gap between them is the economic surplus.
It can be estimated with choice experiments or asked directly in contingent valuation surveys.
Formally, it is the payment that makes a person's utility after an unwanted change, with compensation, equal to their utility before it.
Which measure applies depends on property rights: if lakeside residents have a right to a clean lake, their willingness to accept compensation for pollution counts.

title: WTA–WTP gap
article: Willingness to accept#Standard theory versus experimental results

definition.text: The finding that people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it, even though standard theory predicts the two amounts should match.

facts.text: Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely found willingness to accept for basketball tickets was more than 10 times willingness to pay.
Explanations include income limits on what people can pay and the endowment effect, where owning something triggers loss aversion.
Plott and Zeiler argued the gaps partly reflect participants misunderstanding the experimental task.
The gap matters for contingent valuation, where endowment effects are widespread.

contested_note: Researchers disagree whether the gap reflects real loss aversion or flaws in experimental design.
notes: Endowment effect page gives 14 times for the Carmon and Ariely tickets (S:7d48828611ef), compatible with 'more than 10 times'.
